card.title: Part four checkpoint
card.blurb: The final checkpoint: libraries, the standard library, packages, dependencies and version control. Pass it to wrap up the software foundations.
hero.title: Part four checkpoint
intro.0: The last checkpoint of the theory track. Answer a handful of questions on Part four - libraries, packages, dependencies and version control - to lock it in and earn your XP.
quiz.title: Part four checkpoint
quiz.metaLabel: The development world · Part four checkpoint
quiz.intro: Seven questions drawn from Part four - the world you build in. Pick the best answer for each, then submit. Score five or more to pass and earn XP; a fresh set is drawn each time you retry.
question.1.stem: Why pull in a library instead of writing everything yourself?
question.1.option.0: To reuse tested code others wrote, so you build faster and safer
question.1.option.1: Libraries make the CPU run faster
question.1.option.2: You must - code will not run without one
question.1.option.3: To hide your own code from others
question.1.why: A library is ready-made, tested code you can build on, so you do not reinvent common work.
question.2.option.0: The useful code that ships with the language itself
question.2.option.2: The first file you write in a project
question.2.why: The standard library comes with the language - common tools available without installing anything.
question.3.option.0: A bundle of code you can pull into your project
question.3.why: A package is shareable code you add to your project to get features you did not write.
question.4.stem: What fetches packages - and the packages they depend on - for you?
question.4.why: A package manager downloads the packages you ask for plus their own dependencies.
question.5.stem: Your project needs library X in order to build. X is called a...?
question.5.why: Code your project relies on is a dependency; the package manager makes sure it is present.
question.6.stem: What does version control give you?
question.6.option.0: A tracked history of every change, so you can look back or undo
question.6.why: Version control records changes over time so you can review history and recover earlier versions.
question.7.option.0: A saved snapshot of the project at a point in time
question.7.option.1: A program that is currently running
question.7.why: A commit records the state of the project, with a message, as one step in its history.
question.8.stem: Why is a project's history useful?
question.8.option.0: You can see what changed and return to an earlier version
question.8.option.1: It makes the app run faster
question.8.option.3: It compiles the code for you
question.8.why: The history is a record of every commit, so you can trace changes and roll back if needed.
question.9.stem: How do several people work on one project without overwriting each other?
question.9.option.0: Version control tracks and merges everyone's commits
question.9.option.1: They email files back and forth
question.9.option.2: Only one person may write code at a time
question.9.why: Version control lets each person commit their work and merges the changes together.
question.10.stem: Why open a branch before trying a risky change?
question.10.option.0: It gives you a separate line of commits, so the working version stays safe
question.10.option.1: It makes the code compile faster
question.10.option.3: It emails the change to your team
question.10.why: A branch is your own line of commits that splits off from the main one, so you can experiment without touching the version that works.
question.11.stem: What does merging a branch do?
question.11.option.0: Brings its commits back into the main line, joining the two histories
question.11.option.2: Renames every file in the project
question.11.why: Merging joins a branch's commits back into the main line, so the finished work becomes part of the shared history.
question.12.stem: What is a remote in version control?
question.12.option.0: A shared copy of the history on a server that the whole team pushes to and pulls from
question.12.option.1: A faster CPU for building code
question.12.option.2: A backup that only you can see
question.12.option.3: A tool that writes commits for you
question.12.why: A remote is a shared copy of the history, often hosted on a platform like GitHub, so a team works through one agreed place.
